speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. I believe that when we adjourned yesterday the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) had the floor.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
yesterday as I listened to the address of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) I was reminded of an editorial which appeared in one of the financial papers at the commencement of 1970. It was written at a time when the official opposition had decided to run in the wake of the well informed criticism of the white paper which was then developing.
The editorial gave credit to the official opposition for its political acumen in choosing the white paper as a target but raised a serious question by way of caution. It asked the official opposition and its leader what would happen if that target were removed. Of course, that is what has happened and we now see the sense of frustration, disappointment and confusion which shines through the comments which thus far the official opposition have made on this major budget proposal. They look like the mighty guns of Singapore which, when the battle was joined, were pointing the wrong way and firing at the wrong target.
There was a dichotomy in the address of the hon.
member for Edmonton West. He seemed unable to make up his mind whether to take credit for the good things which are disclosed in this budget or to retreat into the traditional opposition posture of criticizing everything which the government has proposed. And at the end of his remarks I regret to say that his attitude was unclear and the issue appeared to be unresolved in his mind. But as is so often the case, whatever may be said by the official spokesmen of the opposition they are disconcerted and undermined by their colleague, the distinguished member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees). He at least has recognized the wisdom of this budget. He has recognized its immense popularity. He has predicted an election. I understand from the press that he is wagering large amounts of a valuable fluid in support of his prediction. Perhaps the caution should be offered to him that the budget does not propose any reduction in the tax on spirits.
From the NDP we have had what might be expected to be their accustomed response. They must look askance at anything which is popular, at anything which relieves large sections of the population from taxation, and they have looked upon this budget with their accustomed attitude of moral disdain. A remarkable phrase was uttered by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) in his speech yesterday. He described the budget as being "a political budget beyond the point of decency." All of us know that the real translation of those words is that this is a popular budget beyond the reach of his ill-tempered criticism.
Against all the evidence, the NDP will continue to say that this is a budget which is oppressive against the little man in this country, and favours large interests. It is significant that in elaborating this argument yesterday the hon. member for Waterloo, as recorded at page 7231

June 23, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Blair
of Hansard, chose to make a comment about the impact of corporation taxes under the white paper and under the budget proposals. He made the observation that the increase in corporate taxation under the white paper was bound to be far greater than under the current budget proposals. But he failed to point out that more than 60 per cent of the increase in corporate tax envisaged by the white paper arose from the proposal to eliminate the differential tax rate from small corporations, and I suppose we are to take it from that that he and his party oppose this welcome measure of relief, this recognition of the practical problems of small companies.
I also think he could have given a complete picture by dealing fully with the impact of all the proposals in the white paper. The white paper discloses that had the concept of corporate integration with personal income been adopted, after a period of years the treasury would have lost something like $230 million of revenue-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Baloney!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) says "Baloney," but he himself used these figures extensively to prove that there was going to be overtaxation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is right, overtaxation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In any event, this was the amount of revenue which would have been foregone. This is the benefit that the white paper would have conferred upon corporations and their shareholders. I am suggesting that the budget proposals apply equally to benefit all sections of the population. I would not like to have the task of the NDP in attempting to prove to the people of Canada that, as they claim, this budget discriminates against little people, when more than one million are going to be removed from the tax rolls and 4,700,000 more will achieve significant tax reductions. In order to sell this bill of goods to the Canadian people they will require even more Waffle than they presently have in their party.
It is quite clear that we are going to be faced with a tedious semantic argument perhaps from both the opposition parties. The burden of this argument is that the budget proposals do not constitute tax reform. Mr. Speaker, we should consider this allegation carefully. How can we say that a budget that for the first time imposes a capital gains tax is not a major tax reform? How can we say that a budget that accomplishes an immense shifting of the burden of taxation from the low-income brackets is not a major tax reform? How can we say that a budget that for the first time recognizes the position of working wives and mothers by providing for child care deductions is not a major tax reform? How can we say that a budget which provides positive encouragement, as the hon. member for Waterloo himself admitted yesterday, for Canadian ownership is not a major tax reform?
How can we say this about a budget which cuts through the immense complexity of special rules applying to special corporations and their shareholders? How

can we say this about a budget which provides enlightened administrative procedures for which many people have been asking for years?
I think the judgment which will be made upon this budget is that it constitutes the most major reform in the philosophy of our tax structure and the thrust of tax policy since income tax was first introduced in Canada in 1917.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That was a bad bill.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think the greatest significance of this budget is that it brings to a conclusion a period of almost ten years of unsettling discussion about tax reform. We should be clear about the origins of that discussion, Mr. Speaker. There are many people in the chamber and certainly many outside who will recall that this discussion commenced when the government of the day, of which some hon. gentlemen opposite were members, was unable to deal effectively with the problems of taxation arising from the distribution of surpluses of corporations. That government found itself unable to achieve a practical settlement of that problem, and the record is clear that the Carter commission was finally appointed in order to lift the burden of this responsibility from its back.
One of the most significant reforms envisaged by the present budget is a practicable, just and sensible solution of the problem of distribution of corporate surpluses.
An. hon. Member: Opportunities for waste!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Bonaventurel

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Once the royal commission was appointed the country was inexorably committed to a long discussion on tax reform. It was appointed in 1962, it reported in 1967 and since that time the sweeping and important report which it presented has been the focus of tax discussion in Canada. The real significance of the budget is that it brings this long and unsettling discussion to an end. We had reached a critical stage in Canada when many important decisions were being postponed, but now the air has been cleared. The budget proposals may not please everybody, but the element of uncertainty has been removed and the proposals themselves are capable of being understood and applied within the traditional structure of our Income Tax Act. Psychologically, this is the most important feature of the budget. Coupled with the incentives which will be given by way of tax relief and the positive assertion of government policy that the aim of the fiscal policy is to foster development and to encourage enterprise, we now provide a solid platform for unimpeded progress in this country.
I should add, Mr. Speaker, that there is another important policy still to be disclosed. I believe it is important for the government, at the earliest possible date, to make an announcement of its policy with regard to foreign ownership I observe that while this matter is outstanding some decisions are being postponed and some uncertainty is created.
June 23, 1971

In passing, we should note the positive measures which have been taken in this budget in a practical, nondiscriminatory and sensible way to encourage Canadian ownership of our businesses. These include the provision for the deduction of interest paid on money used to acquire shares in Canadian companies, the provision that 90 per cent of the assets of pension and similar funds provided by Canadians shall be invested in Canadian enterprises, the very sensible provisions made for the alteration of the withholding taxes, the provision regarding small companies where the favourable differential rate of taxation applies only to Canadian companies and the solution for distribution of surpluses which is available to Canadian companies.
I suggest that in this long process of discussion of tax policy, we in Parliament and the people of this country have learned a great deal about ourselves. We are essentially a pragmatic and practical people. It is quite obvious now that this nation does not find acceptable the grand, schematic proposals for the over-all alteration of established institutions. These may have great academic appeal, but in terms of our history and tradition it is quite clear that they do not appeal to the typical Canadian. I suppose one might say about the tax structure and the tax system that the decision of the majority of our countrymen is that they like better the devil they know than the devil unknown.
Another feature which develops out of this long discussion is a recognition of the diverse nature of our country which is really too big and too varied to be moved by one theory or one simplistic tax structure. As a consequence, I welcome, as do other hon. members, the fact that differential tax treatment will continue where necessary- where it is necessary, for example, to encourage development in outlying areas, where it is necessary to encourage development of the mining and petroleum industries. The budget also recognizes the special position of different types of corporations such as co-operatives and credit unions in which, as many hon. members know, I have had a lifelong interest.
In regard to all these changes which have been proposed I must say that it is impossible at this time to make comments on the immense draft bill which we have received. However, there are bound to be some areas of the bill which require clarification, and I hope that all members of the House will join in trying to produce the best bill possible so that our fellow citizens who are taxpayers will be able to apply a simple and well-worded law to their affairs.
There are other things about the budget which give me great personal satisfaction and which remove the pall which had been cast upon very deserving people in our country. I mention, for example, the decision not to subject personal residences to a capital gains tax. I also call attention to the change in the income tax rates which make it possible now to say that those people who during the great discussion were called the middle-income group and whose incomes were over $10,000 will not be subjected to higher absolute taxation. I have mentioned before the exceedingly important practical decision to deal with
The Budget-Mr. Blair
the troublesome question of the distribution of corporate surpluses.
The hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Kaplan) referred to some of the political consequences of the long investigative and deliberative process which went on, particularly in the consideration of the white paper. Speaking for myself, I cannot think of any national discussion which has been more intensive and more comprehensive. There will now be nobody who dares to say, as was said during the course of those discussions, that the government would not listen. In a sense, the new proposals represent a triumph of democracy. I am quite convinced they have been advanced as the result of important work done by the House of Commons Committee on Finance. We are all indebted to the members of that committee for their work and their report, because it undoubtedly provided the effective foundation for the budget.
Apart from these important income tax changes which in a sense have obscured other vital changes in the budget, I would like to comment very briefly on some of the changes made in tariffs, sales and excise taxes. I welcome the decision of the government to alter the tariff rates affecting the production of polyethylene, not only because of the support it will give to this important segment of the chemical industry, but because of the hope that it holds out for the petrochemical industry, in particular, of government interest, participation and cooperation in solving its many difficulties. These difficulties were expounded yesterday by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin). I am sure all members were as happy as I was to hear him again re-emphasize the recognition of the problems of the industry and his determination to assist in their solution.
The petrochemical industry deserves the support of this Parliament because it is one of the most technologically advanced industries in our country. We must keep abreast of this technology in order to prosper as a modern industrial society. The same comments can be made about the electronics industry which will be greatly assisted by the removal of the special 15 per cent excise tax which has applied to a wide range of consumer electronic products. In making this change, the government has not only responded to producing companies in the industry but to their unions. As is always the case when a mammoth tax deduction such as this is announced on budget night, some hardship and inconvenience can result. I know that there are many retailers who have an expensive inventory of electronic products upon which the tax has been paid. Many of these people are reasonably small businessmen and cannot afford any substantial loss.
I hope that two things will occur. I hope that the government will give consideration to their position and, more important, that the major producers in the electronics industry, who have for so long and so effectively urged this important reform, will not stand aside and let the burden of it be borne entirely by their retail distributors.

June 23, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
As hon. members know, I represent a constituency containing both consumers and dairy producers. The removal of sales tax on margarine eliminates an anomaly in our law, it having been the only food product upon which sales tax was charged. It will be of immense benefit to consumers of margarine. However, I suggest that the effect of the change must be carefully watched. Under the leadership of this government great progress has been made in the current year in achieving greater stability in the dairy industry and in improving the financial returns to dairy producers. Notwithstanding this, they still face difficulties. I do not think they are in a position to absorb many reverses. If any momentary adverse effects occur as a result of this tax change, I hope that other measures will be taken to protect them so that the progress achieved this year will not be undone.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair). While he had quite strong praise of a general nature for the budget, it seemed that by the time he was through he was just as worried about some of the things it had done as he was pleased about some of its other measures. I can only sum it by saying that he thanked God the process was over, he hoped, and the results were not as bad as they may have been.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hope the expression used by the hon. member, indicating that the discussion was over, does not mean it is the intention of the majority of this House to prevent further discussion on these matters. I am sure he did not mean that.
Today we are discussing two documents that are of vital concern to the Canadian people. Each one in its own way expresses the intentions or alleged intentions of the federal government in terms of economic policy. Each is an indication of what we can expect to happen or not happen in the future. Each indicates or purports to indicate the direction that the government expects and hopes the economy will go.
The tax amendment package is one such document. It purports to set forth the long-term policy proposals purporting to create an equitable and realistic tax framework within which the Canadian economy can grow and prosper. The tax reform package purports to be an expression of both the government's long-term economic predictions and its economic philosophy. It purports to tell us something about both the expectations and the goals of the government. After years of indecision and uncertainty, referred to with some emphasis by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, at least we are now being given what purports to be the government's blueprint for the future, although as I go along I will express some doubts about how much it really means as a blueprint for the future.
If the tax amendment proposals purport to give us a long-term idea of the government's intentions, the actual budget for the fiscal year which was announced last
Friday tells us what the immediate short-term approaches of the government are. In terms of the budget, we are no longer in the realm of intentions or possibilities some time in the future. We must never forget that intentions can change even if they are honestly stated. In terms of the budget, we are in the realm of the immediate. This is the government supposedly in action. The way in which the government now acts must surely tell us something more concrete about its real intentions than all the words in which those intentions are couched either by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) or by anybody else.
The so-called tax reform package is the government's purporting to tell us its future plans, but the budget is the government's acting out its plans in terms of the needs and contexts of the day. That is why in this debate we have to pay considerable attention to the budget for the current fiscal year as distinct from the proposals relating to 1972 and subsequent years. The budget is vitally important both for what it does and does not do to help the economy now. It is also very important in terms of shedding some light on the real, as opposed to the pretended, score sheet of this government.
Let me say immediately that there are some things which I welcome and there are others to which I simply take no objection. I certainly favour the elimination of the 3 per cent surtax. We on this side of the House have been calling for its removal for the past year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Harm which could be mitigated.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It could be mitigated. I said it might do harm in certain circumstances, as the hon. member him-

June 23, 1971

self said a few minutes ago, to people who are caught holding certain inventories. But I am not quarrelling with these proposals to reduce excise tax, nor am I intent on opposing other similar minor items in the budget.
I suppose one could call the removal of the tax on margarine a confusion of products, as it is obviously an attempt to "butter up" consumers. An inveterate eater of margarine might save up to 25 cents a week, assuming he were to dispose of close to a pound a day. I can only assume that the government has concluded that the abolition of this tax will not have much effect on our butter producers; it certainly will not do much to help consumers or lower the cost of living.
The total tax relief to be envisaged for individual Canadians for the balance of the year amounts to some $135 million of which no less than $90 million is accounted for by the removal of a surtax which was supposed to have been removed on December 31, 1970, in any event. In other words, the real income tax reduction for Canadians with lower incomes and older Canadians amounts to some $45 million, about one-third of one per cent of the budget, a paltry and perhaps even an insulting amount, the equivalent of $2 a year for each Canadian. As for other Canadian taxpayers generally, they are not to be given any real tax relief in spite of the attempt by the government to conjure up such an illusion. It is true the corporations are expected to pay some $255 million less in corporate income tax this fiscal year than they did in the last. In other words, the revenue from corporate income tax will be down by about 10 per cent-about 7 per cent more than is accounted for by the removal of the surtax. I presume this is likely to be the result of an anticipated drop in corporate profits during the year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They pay taxes in the current year on last year's profits.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: For individual taxpayers the results are different. According to the government's figures, personal income tax will be up by $838 million during the present fiscal year which ends on March 31, 1972. This represents an over-all increase of 13 per cent in tax paid by individuals in the present fiscal year as compared with the fiscal year ended March 31 last. In other words, while the minister pretends to be reducing personal income tax by taking off the 3 per cent surtax, he will really be collecting 13 per cent more from personal income tax payers.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is in the fine print.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is the information the minister gave out.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: More taxpayers.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is not necessarily a tax reduction. If the minister had not changed the tax rate to the extent he has, he would have collected another $255 million this year in addition to what he intends to take under his present proposals.
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
Somebody, somewhere, has called this an expansionary budget. Certainly the taxes collected from individual taxpayers will expand, but compared with the needs of this country in terms of unemployment and the urgency of stimulating the economy this budget is worse than ineffective, it is simply irrelevant.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The tax reductions are not sufficient to make any impact. The Minister of Finance seems to think a little dab will do it. A little dab may be all right for his hair, it may be all right for my hair, but it is not good enough for the economy of the country in the year 1971.
What I find interesting in all this talk about expansion is the alacrity with which the government has seized upon the adjective "expansionary". They have come to love the word. I find this all the more interesting because up to now the minister has been telling the Canadian people that the economy is already expanding satisfactorily. There is no need, he said, for special measures to get the economy moving again; there is no need for any special concern.
If that is indeed the case, I must ask the Minister of Finance why he chose to make even these few small gestures to stimulate the economy. And having made them, why is he now so proud of them? If these measures were not required last December, why are they considered necessary now? The minister has been saying for months that things have been going well. I suggest he is taking action now because he knows perfectly well in his heart that the economy is not moving forward satisfactorily in terms of reducing unemployment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would refer the Minister of Finance to a paper put out recently by the Institute of Quantitative Analysis of Social and Economic Policy, an institution, part of the University of Toronto, which the Minister of Finance mentioned when talking a few days ago about agencies in Canada which made short-term economic forecasts. The reference is a paper entitled "Policy options for high employment without inflation." In it we are told that even if the gross national product of Canada should increase by 5 per cent this year, as predicted in the paper, it would still mean a decline in unemployment of only one-quarter of one per cent.
This is exactly the point I have been trying to drum into the head of the Minister of Finance for months. The Economic Council of Canada has been telling us for years we need real growth of that order just to enable us to hold our own against further increases in the rate of unemployment. I wonder whether the minister has taken that forecast into consideration. It is a question we may well ask. I suggest that if the minister and the government had really thought the economy was moving forward satisfactorily, not only would they not have lowered tax rates-and I accept here help for low-income people because even people with hearts as cold as the heart of this government would have moved to do something for the low-income people anyway

but they would

June 23, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
not be describing this as a policy of expansion. They cannot have it both ways. They cannot say at one and the same time that their past policies have worked and also claim that there is need for expansion at the present time. At least, they cannot say it and expect to be believed.
How are we to believe that the Minister of Finance is any more accurate about the taxes he proposes to collect in 1972 and 1973, if by any disaster it is still his responsibility then, than he has been in his dismally inaccurate forecasts for the six months just past? Where is the minister's consistency of approach? On the one hand he tells us that he has to budget frequently, perhaps several times a year, to deal realistically with changing conditions. On the other hand he simultaneously presents a future budget revenue package that he characterizes as historic and lasting.
Are we to take it from this that he has abandoned the flexibility that has thus far been his excuse for bungling? Of course not, Mr. Speaker. This Minister of Finance would not abandon anything for an excuse like that. Is it not more likely that six months from now he intends to depart from the proposed package as dramatically as the package itself departs from the proposals in his white paper of 1969?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think he should depart altogether.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That would save a lot of problems. Let us just look at the record, Mr. Speaker. For the past few months the minister has been telling the House and trying to convince the Canadian people that he has not really been defending the proposals in his white paper. "Who me?", asks the minister. "I am just a simple country boy trying to get a dialogue going. Far be it for me to try to bulldoze the Canadian people into any particular kind of tax reform. No, Sir!"
This is the image that the minister has been trying to project during the last three months and he has been doing so for a very good reason. He has come to know very well, to realize at last-indeed, he has known this for a few months now-that there is not the ghost of a chance of the Canadian people going along with many of the original proposals in his white paper. This, Mr. Speaker, is the new Minister of Finance, a man who is reasonable and friendly, like a cocker spaniel. Why, you can almost see him wagging his tail. But the minister was not always like this. When the white paper was tabled 18 months ago it was the proud father who faced us then, but who quickly turned into a pretty fierce watchdog defending every inch of terrain from the critics he dismissed as mere upstarts and as, generally speaking, representatives of large interests. The minister now blandly announces that he will not, of course, do anything to hurt the small business corporations. He is going to retain the concessions that the white paper was going to abolish.
Listen to what the minister said at an earlier time, Mr. Speaker. According to the Minister, in 1967 over 450,000
Canadians paid tax on their business profits at personal rates because they were unincorporated. This group included about 50,000 doctors, lawyers and other professionals who are barred from incorporating. However, said the minister, this left 400,000 other businessmen who did not get any benefit from the low corporate tax rate- "These, I believe, are the real small businesses in Canada". This was one of the reasons the minister refused to sanction anything even approaching the measure he is now putting forward protecting a lower corporate tax rate for incorporated businesses below a certain size, and was his defence then for increasing taxes on small corporations. He delivered that speech in tones as convincing as he could make them.
Has the minister changed his mind since then? He now accepts what he then rejected and rejects what he accepted.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Think about it, Ben; it will come to you.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Has the minister really changed his mind?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Sure.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He has not told us so. Does he really
intend to stick to these changes, to his present recommendations, if the government should-God forbid-win another election? Who can tell, Mr. Speaker? For the time being the Minister of Finance has swallowed his
own principles, if that is what they were.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is something better.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hon. members opposite were just as pleased with the white paper when it was first brought in as they are pleased with this budget. I can readily understand why hon. members are so happy. When a fellow like the Minister of Finance has been banging their heads against the wall for a year and a half, it must feel pretty good when he stops.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That was not the only principle that he shunted aside; there were a host of others. There was the five-year revaluation tax on widely held shares; he defended that in eloquent terms. There was the full income tax rate generally applied to capital gains with the exception of widely held shares. There was the extension of this tax to the family home and all the other proposals that he first adopted as his own, only to discard them reluctantly as the months and years wore on.
Why did the minister do this, Mr. Speaker? I think the answer is pretty simple: He did it because he finally realized that politically there was nothing to gain and everything to lose. He did it not because he had been convinced by the opposition or by anybody else that what he was proposing was wrong; he did it because he realized that the proposals were unpopular. Why did the chicken cross the road, Mr. Speaker? Ask the Minister of Finance.

June 23, 1971

Let us take another example. The minister grandly announced on Friday the death of death duties as far as the federal government was concerned. But listen to what the same minister said on February 13, 1969, not very long before the white paper on tax reform was introduced:
More than $200 million a year is raised through the estate tax and provincial succession duties.
Any mistakes in grammar can be attributed to the minister and not me, because I am trying to read the quotation faithfully. It continues as follows:
Some critics might argue that we could do away with this kind of tax if governments tightened their belts and reduced spending by this amount. Our conclusion is that the government feels that the estate tax is a fair and equitable part of our total tax system regardless of the revenues we need.
That was said by the Minister of Finance a few months before he introduced his white paper on tax reform.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is no change.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Could there be anything clearer than that-anything, that is, other than the decision of the very same minister and the government to do away with the tax as announced last Friday? There is consistency for you! In 1969 before the introduction of the white paper-and the government must have had a little bit of advice about tax reforms-the minister put the country through a lot of turmoil and trouble by an increase in estate taxes in an attempt to reduce the tax on very small estates. Now, with great fanfare the minister announces its abolition, also for the very best of reasons.
Then there is the affair of the 3 per cent surtax on personal and corporate taxes. We had the Minister of Finance assuring us in the beginning that this was a temporary measure and would disappear by the end of last year. We had the firm assurance of the minister in this regard. Last December we had the same minister tell us in urgent tones that any move to abolish the surtax was sure to bring on inflation. He took up quite a bit of time in the House telling us about the surtax situation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister is leaving; he can't take it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think he can take it and I would not make that charge against him. I want to emphasize in particular that at the very time the Minister of Finance was saying the 3 per cent tax could not be removed because it was inflationary, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) went into another room and he said inflation was licked. Six months later the minister comes back with a flourish and abolishes the 3 per cent surtax at a time when inflation is not licked and, according to his own statement, the economy is moving forward faster than ever. There is something here that smells, and it is not a rose.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is your locker-room.
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend certainly has a locker-room smell. One just has to look at the way he retreated from the white paper to know how it smelled to him. So much for integrity!
Let us look more closely at predictions. On December 12, 1968, the minister assured this House there would be a balanced budget. It turned out to be a deficit of some $300 million. In 1969, before the budget, the minister gave an assurance that unemployment was declining. In December, 1970, when introducing his budget the Minister of Finance said among other things that employment was rising in Canada and unemployment on a seasonally adjusted basis appeared to be falling. That was in December of 1970, and on the same day on the television program "Encounter" the minister said:
The trend will be downward in unemployment in Canada seasonally adjusted through next year.
On the same day the minister said he was willing to bet that unemployment on a seasonally adjusted basis would progressively decline throughout 1971.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I still do.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not quite two months later, on the program "Question Period" on January 31 the minister said:
Our trend is down and I think our trend will continue downwards in 1971.
On February 25 he was predicting a mid-year economic upturn, and on March 11 he told us:
I believe that in the fiscal year 1971-72 we will find a decline in seasonally adjusted unemployment.
I notice that each time he speaks the minister shows certain tendencies. He tends to put off the promised fall in seasonally adjusted unemployment to a little later. First of all this fall in unemployment was supposed to take place throughout the year 1971, then it was supposed to take place by mid-year, and finally the minister was talking about the fiscal year 1971-72 which we have just started. He said all this in spite of the fact we know the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate of unemployment was higher in May than the rate for last January.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: By one-tenth of one per cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, by one-tenth of one per cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was .6 per cent lower than September.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister is now saying this does not amount to anything more than one-tenth of one per cent, but how could anybody in Canada take this minister or his predictions seriously? How can we give him any more credit in respect of his predictions for the future than he deserves in regard to the past?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Because he can live on $30 a week.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No matter how hard they try, the gentlemen of this government cannot retain their credibility for long on this issue. The magnitude of the credibility gap of this government is enormous. It makes the Grand

June 23, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
Canyon look like a hairline crack. So much for cracks about hairlines. The new heights of arrogance and complacency displayed by this government make the Rocky Mountains look like a fluctuation. It seems that we now have before us a new "incredible" Canadian.
The minister has had a great deal of difficulty with his predictions in respect of the financial position of the government. I have mentioned the 1968-69 experience. On March 12 of 1970 the minister forecast a budget surplus in the order of $300 million.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There were four changes after that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There were four changes, but last December that had become a deficit forecast of $320 million, and last Friday it was a deficit of some $420 million. This is a mere error of $720 million since the first prediction.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not true.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We might well have been talking to the wind. The results are before us. They show a government which on this issue is still incapable of listening either to others or to the economic indicators it has in front of it. They show a government that is as stubborn and as blind as ever on this issue. They show a government that refuses to listen and refuses to act in any meaningful way to get the economy rolling again. How, one might ask, does this square with the tax reform legislation this same government has brought in?
Here we have a government that is in full retreat all along the line. Here we have a government which gave the appearance of having listened to reason. This is a government of humility, of sweet reason, a government which has learned from dialogue and which has responded to public opinion. Mr. Speaker, I do not have to go over the catalogue of retreat in the white paper. I think the disappearance of these things is good. We accept these changes and in association with others accept a considerable proportion of credit for having brought forward the suggestions and for having brought about the changes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

June 23, 1971

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why did all your members abstain from voting in the committee?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must admit, however, that certain suspicions remain. It is true the government has been forced to retreat, but it has retreated in disorder. The Minister of Finance's rather peevish remarks last Friday night about the failure to integrate corporation taxes were an indication of this. Everybody was at fault but the government. The government knows best but nobody was willing to listen, complained the minister. That is an old song with this government. The difference is that on this occasion the government pretends to have listened to the people and changed its intentions. Or has it merely changed its tactics?
I would remind this House that unlike the budget for the current year the tax package is really nothing but an expression of intentions under which the government, virtually at will, can change the rates of tax. Specifically, they can be changed at any time by the simple device of adding a surtax, which this government knows so well how to do. Even that may not be necessary.
Mr. Speaker, one can have no confidence at all that the rates set forth in the minister's proposals for 1972, 1973 and so on will in fact be the rates of tax paid by the Canadian people. One could have no confidence at all in this, that is, if this government continues to hold office. There just is no credibility there in view of past performance. The government promises to lower taxes for most people in 1972 and after that. What does this mean in fact? It is true that under these proposals for the year 1972, for example, there will be fewer people on the tax rolls. That is good to see. I am glad to see the increase in exemptions particularly in respect of the aged, and I am glad to see the provision for deducting expenses for the working man. I do not think I would have had a ceiling of $150 on this, although I am glad to see it.
I assure the minister that these things will be discussed in detail. I am glad to see these changes, although they could be improved. It is true, also, that the tax rate proposed on the first $500 of taxable income is supposed to come down over a period of years from 17 per cent to 6 per cent, if the government sticks to what it says. But, Mr. Speaker, the so-called tax reform package as a whole is a camouflage operation, because once you are on the tax rolls and once you earn more than $500 of taxable income, then of course you run into rates of taxation substantially above the rates of taxation for those brackets today. A person with $1,000 of taxable income who now pays $150 would pay $227.50, and a person with $2,000 of taxable income who now pays $351.50 would pay $474.50.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Taxable income.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I made it very clear that I am talking about taxable income. There is no need for anybody to resort to any misrepresentation.
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Listen and you will hear something.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What I am suggesting to the minister, and what the people of Canada should understand clearly, is that it is people with taxable incomes between $500 and $10,000 a year who will really get the wallop. The Prime Minister suggested as recently as yesterday that it is the wealthy who will pay the increased taxes in this country.
It is not the wealthy people I am talking about. Certainly a taxable income of $2,000 does not give you a very good entry into the jet set. These are ordinary Canadians of average income, and yet they will pay heavier taxes on every bit of increased taxable income which they will earn through 1972, 1973, 1974, and so on. As the years go on and as inflation and productivity go up, it is inevitable that more and more Canadians with modest incomes-and this will come very quickly-will see an ever-increasing proportion of their income taken by the government in income taxation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Your deputy minister should have told you that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister shakes his head, but he cannot deny it. He cannot deny that the rates on taxable income at the level between $500 and $10,000 a year are substantially higher in his new proposals than the existing tax rate. This means, inevitably, that as the ordinary, average Canadian works his way up a little, either as a result of inflation or as a result of moving ahead he will get a much harder "whammy" than he gets under the existing tax rate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. I assume the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) is rising for the purpose of asking a question. This can be done only with the consent of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) who has the floor.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sure the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) would not want to mislead anyone. Does he know that according to the new proposal a taxpayer with two dependants whose income moves up from $2,800 even up to $50,000 would pay less tax than he pays under the present system, no matter how much his income goes up?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nonsense.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I repeat the statement. There is no question that this is what will happen and this is what produces the money, for example, that may enable the government to reduce corporation taxes as it proposes to do. They refer to this in technical terms as the greater elasticity of the system. Your rates move up much more rapidly, particularly between the levels of $1,000 taxable income and $10,000 taxable income. If, for example, you take someone with a $15,000 taxable income a year, his rates will be about the same as they are now. I am not

June 23, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
suggesting that capital gains taxes will be lower, but I am saying as emphatically as I can that this tax package will catch the average Canadian very quickly.
It follows that people with taxable incomes between $1,000 and $10,000 are the ones who will be hit, and it is a false presentation to give to the people of Canada these figures for the year 1972. Therefore, it is necessary for people like myself, and others, to point out exactly what will happen to them under this tax package.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Robin Hood in reverse.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is a misleading presentation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are trying to mislead the people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister knows these things perfectly well. He knows that what I am saying is perfectly correct.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not true.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The word "elasticity" is a $30 word, one of those chromium push-button words that the government likes to come up with, I suppose to disguise this kind of hidden "whammy." You have to constantly watch for these words that are used to cover up some kind of ambush.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Underwear language.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They snap back.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is right, they snap back. It means something stretched

but the kind of stretching that goes on here is neither simple nor innocent. I admit it is a simple thing so far as underwear is concerned, but in characterizing this tax change as giving the average Canadian a better break, the Minister of Finance is stretching the truth. Perhaps the word is just meant to convey the truth. Perhaps you get a break coming out of the gate, but you will be clobbered in the stretch. This is exactly what will happen.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is the reality that faces the ordinary, average Canadian. He will find it much harder to work his way up in real terms. He will find the government of Canada taking a much bigger percentage of his income as it increases as a result of inflation or through the normal process. It is important that the Canadian people understand this.
I repeat again that there is no reason in the world to believe that if the Minister of Finance continues in his position the tax rates set forth in his proposals will in fact be the tax rates that the people will pay in 1972. Of course, the minister could not stand up here and give any assurance that these will be the rates in effect in 1972, and if for one reason or another as a result of his frequent budgeting he will not change his taxes owing to what he considers to be the necessity of the economy, this is what will happen.
When one looks at the document as presented to us as a tax reform, one thing stands out. I do not want to get involved in semantics; the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton suggested that we should avoid this. This is not really a tax reform at all. Certainly I am very happy that some of the more insane measures have been taken out. But what we are left with is a series of measures that can only be called tax reform by courtesy. As the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton said he hoped, we will have a good deal to say about these specific measures as they come forward. But this is not the time for that.
I ask whether what we now have before us is really the result of some years of work, two or three years at least of frustration and uncertainty and public debate. Is this what business, labour and farmers were put through the wringer for in connection with the white paper? Is this the reason for which time, money and talent were spent? What a waste! True, it is not as bad as it might have been, but why did the Minister of Finance feel it necessary to put the country through all the trouble for this? After all these years, the best the government has been able to do is present something that does not scare the daylights out of everybody. That is some achievement, Mr. Speaker, after years of intensive debate during which the government pretended to take the white paper seriously and in so doing wasted the time and energy of thousands and thousands of Canadians. This government is fond of public relations gimmicks that hide reality. Now it has come up with a new one.
To see the real face of the government we must look at its performance in the present budget. In the midst of massive unemployment it presents an empty, meaningless shell and beside it another one glittering with promises but equally empty. They are both equally worthless and I do not believe the Canadian people will take very long to find this out. Perhaps the government does not intend to give them very long; I don't know. Perhaps this is an election budget, an election package. If it is, then the government is even more cynical than I thought. But it would be in character.
What this country needs is neither election budgets nor promises of pie in the sky. What this country has needed and still needs right now is a budget based upon the goal of a satisfactory rate of employment. What this country needs is not a Minister of Finance who wastes everybody's time with grandiose but completely impractical plans and then rushes off into a disgraceful kind of retreat without even expressing his regrets for the time and the talents that have been wasted. Mr. Speaker, it fits. We have now been through the process of spending three years on constitutional reform and we are told today that the Prime Minister says, "You know, it really isn't very important." That fits too.
What this country needs is a minister who not only knows where he is going but also how he is going to get there. It needs a Minister of Finance who believes in working with others, in the public and private sector alike, to encourage the economy to operate at its full

June 23, 1971

potential for the good of all Canadians. What this country needs in the long run is tax reform that takes into account the need for equity and the need for economic growth. What it needs right now is a policy to permit the economy to push ahead at something close to its full capacity.
It may amuse the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mahoney) that there are about
600,000	Canadians out of work, but I do not find it very funny, Mr. Speaker. What this country needs is not a government that talks of reform but accomplishes nothing and meanwhile creates a climate where uncertainty and distrust destroy the possibility of balanced growth. What this country needs is a government that will work effectively to build confidence and restore sanity, to serve human beings and human dignity. Mr. Speaker, we certainly do not have that kind of government today.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

decision to make at this point. I ask the minister to resume his seat because standing will give him no precedence. The same hon. members, of course, would have an opportunity to make a second speech after we have disposed of the amendment. I would like to know the reaction of the hon. members involved.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would prefer to use the full time allotted to me. If you recognize the minister, that will be fine provided that at the next opportunity for debate I have my full time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I believe that in the circumstances the Chair should recognize the minister, although I am still open to suggestions. I see the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) seeking the floor on this matter.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
was going to make the suggestion that the minister be recognized but that I be permitted to put in a request now that we have two speakers on Friday.
The Budget-Mr. Greene

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think that is a very reasonable request and certainly the Chair sees no objection to it. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On a point of order-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. member for Cape
Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Maclnnis) is rising on a point of order. I bring to the attention of the hon. member that we now have only 25 minutes left. The Leader of the Opposition had over an hour for his speech and I think in fairness other members should be given a chance to make their speeches.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on this occasion only to draw attention to the fact that the procedure usually followed in the House has been one that is going to be violated by the minister. I would call on the minister to take the opportunity, some day when he is not on the roster, to appear in the House and make his speech.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) for his courtesy. I do not intend to attempt to answer sally by sally and witticism by witticism the speech of the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), but I do congratulate him on finding a new gag writer. I think in that respect he has done very well indeed. From the standpoint of valid criticism of the budget, I fear I cannot commend him to the same degree.
I was interested to see that the Leader of the Opposition advocated massive or larger tax cuts without in any way indicating what programs he would abrogate as a result of those tax cuts, or whether in fact he would be satisfied to have an even larger deficit than is envisaged in the budget. This is the kind of responsibility we have learned to expect from the official opposition, namely, never telling the Canadian people the cost or the price of the measures that they advocate. I think the government on that score certainly has indicated its responsibility to the Canadian people. In accord with the directions of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his leadership, we have indicated the price of measures that we advocate and not just the benefits of the measures themselves.
In his criticism the Leader of the Opposition certainly failed to do this. While his criticisms have been very largely negative, I think there have been some criticisms of the government's policies in respect of the budget and prior to the budget, with particular reference to resources, that are worthy of reply and I intend to address the few minutes that I have available to me in that direction.

June 23, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Greene
Mr. Speaker, it was that non-liberal but powerful and highly quotable political figure, Edmund Burke, who said:
To tax and to please,
No more than to love and be wise,
Is not given to man.
I use this quotation because it so aptly illustrates the circumstances in which my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has found himself over the past three years in connection with tax reform. The government made clear its desire to have more inputs from the public of Canada in terms of the major policies which will affect our nation. The Minister of Finance has employed this policy of "participatory democracy" in the government's review of proposed tax reform measures.
It was an awesome burden for my colleague the Minister of Finance to carry and a "first" so far as parliamentary traditions are concerned. Never before have so many people had so much involvement, with so much recognition as in the processes which led to the budget speech by the Minister of Finance in the House on June 18 last. It has been a difficult task and one made at times almost unbearable by the criticisms which have been made at large in the country about tax reform and the government's white paper, which was clearly issued for the purpose of consulting with the people of Canada on the nature of the tax reforms which would be efficacious and acceptable to the community at large.
In all of the circumstances I think the Minister of Finance has carried out his assignment with diligence, forbearance and, finally, with excellent results. He may not be able to tax and to please at the same time, but I am sure that he has done as superb a job of balancing all of the competing interests as could have been done by anyone. It is not in the nature of things politic that he will receive thanks from the country commensurate with the contumely he has received in the process of the participatory exercise. I think it would be valid to go on record today to state that his performance has served the nation well and in the long run will be validated by the course of history.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That sounds like a eulogy.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The tax reform proposals introduced by my colleague the Minister of Finance are indeed of historic importance. The process of their development, beginning in 1962, included opinion and comment from individuals, institutions, industry, the provinces, parliamentary committees and, of course, the Royal Commission on Taxation. The degree of national involvement and the ways in which the proposals are sensitive to a diversity of national needs demonstrate clearly that interested Canadians do have a voice in the formulation of national policies and priorities. The sometimes overworked phrase "participatory democracy" has real meaning.

The proposals also represent a milestone in public policy toward the Canadian mineral industry. Tax incentives undoubtedly played a major role in developing the Canadian mineral industry to its present status as the world's third largest diversified mineral industry. It is now a strong, vigorous industry. We are at the stage, therefore, when it is appropriate to reshape the historic incentives to the industry with a view to making them more efficient and responsive to Canadian needs. The replacement of the three-year exemption for new mines at the end of 1973, and the automatic depletion deduction at the end of 1976 by special accelerated depreciation measures and earned depletion provisions, are major changes with philosophical ramifications. In my view, these specific changes have meant a clear recognition of the importance of this sector to the economy and an appreciation by the government of the need for a measure of continued incentive.

I believe, Mr. Speaker, it is important to underscore the fact that ours is a private enterprise system and that a viable mineral industry is an important generator of output and employment. Let me point out that when I use the term mineral industry I mean to include both the mining and the oil and gas industries. These sources of wealth permit us to pursue other national goals more fully and with greater flexibility.
The retention of special incentives along the lines that reflect more directly the needs of the industry and that relate more closely to over-all mineral policy elements is an important shift; it represents one dimension of the approach to resource policy management by governments. By this I mean that, if minerals are to make a maximum contribution to national development, the specific policy instruments available, including tax policy, must be more finely tuned. The tax proposals for the mining and petroleum industries do reflect the risk involved in mineral ventures, the international competition for capital, the incentives available in other countries, and world market conditions.
The proposals also provide a five-year period in which to plan and adjust to the new system. Also of importance is the fact that profitable ventures will bear a fair share of taxation.

I have made reference to several subjects raised in the tax reform proposals and drawn attention to some broad implications in response to the question of public debate concerned with the management of our non-renewable resources and with the government's policies for those resources. There is a close relationship between minerals and current policy issues on taxation, northern development, foreign ownership and control, rural adjustment, regional disparities, science policy, environmental control, foreign trade and aid, international relations and federal-provincial relations.
We recognize that non-renewable resources are a national heritage and also that mineral-related activities are intertwined throughout a wide spectrum of local,

provincial, regional, national and international issues. However, this accentuates the need to continually keep mineral and energy policy under review. There is a need, for example, to develop comprehensive strategies as a basis for confronting external forces pertaining to corporate strategies of multinational firms, resource procurement strategies of industrial nations and resource development strategies of resource producing nations. All these pertain to and affect Canadian mineral and energy policies and all are interrelated.
Probably one of the key factors is the new ethic in regard to the use of resources. Here I refer to the Christian Science Monitor editorial of Saturday, June 19, 1971, which reads in part as follows:
It may help shock the public into awareness that blindly increasing production and consumption for its own sake is at best wasteful, at worst lethal, and at any time immoral in a world of want. But economic growth is not a faucet to be turned off at will.
The real question, it seems to us, must turn on what kind of growth, for what purpose, for whose benefit, and at what cost? This newspaper has called before for continuing growth in the quality of life rather than in material output. Since production of material goods ultimates in wastes, both as side effect and as end product, the new environmental-age view of the national product must weigh social benefits versus social costs.
In the energy and resources field this is certainly a new ethic rather than the pure form of growth we have known in the past and one to which we must address ourselves in policy-making taxwise and otherwise.
The tax changes proposed by my colleague the Minister of Finance last Friday reflect the importance which the government attaches to healthy, dynamic mineral and energy industries. There are some Canadians who do not subscribe to this view, who state that the industry is capital intensive and is therefore a small employer of labour. Economists have never been entirely right in any of these matters-there are economists, quasi-economists and pseudo-economists, but economists generally have not yet been called to attention as lawyers were when Mr. Bumble said, "The law is a ass". We do not yet know whether economics has achieved that status, but at best it is an imperfect science. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that what is required even in this imperfect science is a faith in the validity of the statistics upon which the conclusions are based.
What is also lacking in these public utterances is a searching analysis of the statistics employed to prove a false thesis. The statistics used, in so far as they go, are satisfactory; they, the statistics, and the analysis of them, just do not go far enough. They become, in effect, half-truths-and half-truths can often be more misleading than simple falsehoods because one can readily distinguish the latter. For one thing, they forget that mineral and energy materials are unique in economic terms in that although they require large amounts of capital for their extraction and processing they are, in turn, a source of capital.
Moreover, they also forget that most of our primary processing and many of our manufacturing establishments exist only because they are based on the produc-
The Budget-Mr. Greene
tion of domestic raw materials. This fact is concealed because the statistical system we employ in Canada is part of an international system, a system designed more for highly developed economies such as those of western Europe, the United States and Japan, economies which are highly deficient in mineral raw materials and which import them from abroad to feed their primary processing and manufacturing plants.
The labour employment widely quoted for the mining industry is 120,000, obviously a small part of the Canadian labour force. Simple analysis indicates just how misleading this figure is. For instance, we have in Canada the world's largest primary nickel processing facilities employing thousands of people in Sudbury, Ontario, Thompson, Manitoba, Port Colborne, Ontario, Fort Saskatchewan, Alberta, and a new facility soon to be constructed on the south shore of the St. Lawrence River in Quebec, all of which produce primary metal products for secondary manufacturing. These primary processing operations exist only because of the domestic mines which feed them; their employment statistics are not included in the widely quoted mining labour statistics.
For a small country in terms of population, we possess the world's twelfth largest primary iron and steel industry, an industry which draws much of its raw material from domestic mines. Do those employed in the blast furnaces and steel works in Sault Ste. Marie, Sydney or Hamilton areas show in the mining labour figure? No. The same holds true for the non-ferrous smelters and refineries and primary processing plants in such widely separated places as Trail, B.C., Flin Flon, Manitoba, Timmins, Ontario, Noranda, Murdochville, Sorel and Valley-field, all in Quebec, and Belledune, N.B. Yet these installations, and many others, which employ thousands of Canadians are all engaged in the further removal of waste material from domestic mineral raw materials, for secondary manufacturing in both Canada and abroad. If we add this employment in primary processing to mining industry employment, the figure of 120,000 for mining industry employment more than doubles to 290,000 those engaged directly in the mineral industry.
Let me turn to another aspect of our mineral industry where simple analysis demonstrates its vital role in the economy as a producer of employment, contrary to those who would say otherwise. A simple statistic which is very often neglected is that nearly one-half of the total revenue freight traffic carried by our railways is composed of minerals and mineral products. A simple figure, but what does it mean in real terms of employment and people? It means the construction and operation of railroads by people, and virtually all rail construction in this country during the past quarter of a century has resulted from mineral projects. It means the manufacture of rails in places such as Sydney, Nova Scotia, and Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario; the manufacture of railway freight cars in places such as Trenton, Nova Scotia, Quebec City and Montreal, Quebec, and Oakville and Hamilton, Ontario; the manufacture of diesel-electric locomotives in such *places as London, Ontario, and Montreal, all employing people.

The Budget-Mr. Greene
It means the movement of coal, potash, iron ore, mineral concentrates and mineral products to either domestic processing plants or to export markets. But minerals move by means other than rail. We possess the world's second largest pipeline network for the movement of oil and gas, using pipe largely made in Canada, by Canadians, in such places as Welland and Sault Ste. Marie, both in Ontario, Regina, Saskatchewan, and Camrose, Alberta. Even in inland water traffic, mineral products, much of them moving to or from processing plants in Canada along such tremendous waterways as the St. Lawrence Seaway and the Mackenzie River system, comprise at least 60 per cent of total Canadian inland water traffic, and ore boats are loaded, unloaded and run by people.
Returning to the employment side of the industry, direct mineral industry employment totals 290,000 persons or 4 per cent of the labour force, and the effect of employment in the mineral industry on employment in other sectors is to increase the number of mineral-dependent workers to nearly 20 per cent of the labour force. This is a more realistic measure of the worth of the Canadian mineral industry in the Canadian labour market.
Canada is a large country with most of us huddled within a long, thin area extending a hundred or so miles north of the Canada-United States border. If it were not for our resource industries, there is not much more of Canada that we would occupy. The mineral industry is in large part responsible for the spatial development of Canada, for the opening up and settlement of our hinterland-Schefferville, Labrador City, Gagnon, Fermont, soon to be, Chibougamau, Val d'Or, Noranda, Mattagami, Timmins, Sudbury, Red Lake, Atikokan, Lynn Lake, Thompson, Flin Flon, Beaverlodge, Grande Cache, Pine Point, Yellowknife, Faro and dozens of other towns scattered across the more remote parts of this great country. These are communities in which Canadians live and work and enjoy themselves, all on the fruits of mineral resource extraction and processing.
